title: Why Not Wire It Direct?
description: A garden hose and a fire hose carry water. Only one of them can put out a real fire — and the difference is the whole reason a motor driver exists.

content.value: A controller pin, like the ones you met in Module 4, can supply maybe 40 milliamps — think of it as a garden hose, useful for watering a small pot. A DC motor under load wants closer to 800 milliamps, sometimes far more when it stalls — a fire hose's worth of flow, by comparison. Try to run a fire hose's demand through a garden hose's supply, and the garden hose simply can't deliver it.

controller pin        ~40 mA available    (garden hose)
DC motor under load   ~800 mA wanted      (fire hose)

40 mA in, 800 mA wanted  ->  the pin can't supply it
                              and trying can damage the pin

Wiring a motor's power leads directly to a GPIO pin isn't just underpowered — it can actually damage the controller. GPIO pins are built to switch small signals, not to survive a motor demanding far more current than they're rated for.

This is exactly why the motor driver from the last lesson exists as a separate chip. The controller's weak 40 mA signal switches the driver's internal transistors — a light touch is all it takes to flip a switch — and the driver, wired straight to the battery, supplies the motor's real 800 mA demand. The controller decides; a part built for higher current does the actual work.

controller  --40mA signal-->  driver chip  --800mA-->  motor
(garden hose worth            (built to pass                (fire hose
 of control)                   fire-hose current)             worth of flow)

This same pattern — a small signal controlling a larger power source, rather than supplying it directly — shows up constantly in electronics. A relay does the same job for even bigger loads, like household appliances.

Key takeaway: a controller pin can supply only a small current, far less than a motor needs. A motor driver bridges that gap — accepting the pin's weak signal but supplying the motor's real current from the battery directly.

quiz.question: Roughly how much current can a controller GPIO pin safely supply?
quiz.explain: GPIO pins are built for small signals, not to power motors — tens of milliamps, not hundreds.

quiz.question: What actually happens if you wire a motor's power leads straight to a GPIO pin?
options: It works fine at reduced speed
The pin can't supply the current the motor wants, and the attempt can damage the controller
The motor simply refuses to spin, with no risk to anything
quiz.explain: It's not just underpowered — pulling far more current than a pin is rated for is a real way to damage it.

quiz.question: In the controller-driver-motor chain, what does the controller actually supply to the driver?
options: A weak signal that switches the driver's internal transistors
Nothing — the driver ignores the controller
quiz.explain: The controller only has to supply enough current to flip a switch. The driver, wired to the battery, supplies the motor's real power.
